However, despite decades of research, the mechanisms underlying the relationships between gender, MA, and math achievement remain largely unclear. One of the reasons is that different types of anxiety and math achievement levels are rarely controlled for.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="DESIGN AND METHODS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">We tested the associations between gender, MA, spatial anxiety, test anxiety, neuroticism, and math achievement in a sample of 269 adults.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">We replicated previous findings that spatial anxiety in areas of navigation and mental manipulation, but not imagery, mediates the relationship between gender and MA. Importantly, in light of previous contradictory findings, we found that math achievement significantly mediated this relationship. Crucially, we found that gender, spatial anxiety, test anxiety, neuroticism, and math achievement together accounted for 66% of the variance in MA, with gender uniquely accounting for only 5%.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSIONS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">The commonly reported gender gap in MA is less pronounced when other anxieties are controlled for, especially given that we did not observe gender differences in the strength of the relationship between MA and math achievement.</AbstractText></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author ValidYN="Y">10.51866/oa.977</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText Label="INTRODUCTION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Night eating syndrome (NES) is an eating disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of night eating, morning anorexia and insomnia. This study aimed to determine the prevalence and association of NES with depression, anxiety, stress, sleep quality and eating disorders among students in Kolej MARA Kuala Nerang (KMKN).</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">A cross-sectional study was conducted on 426 students in KMKN. The calculated minimum sample size was 119. A universal sampling method was used, and data on sociodemographic characteristics, NES, depression, anxiety, stress, sleep quality and eating disorders were collected through online self-reported validated questionnaires including the Night Eating Questionnaire; Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale-21; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index; and Eating Attitudes Test- 26. Data were analysed using IBM SPSS version 22. The chi-square test was used to evaluate the association of NES with sociodemographic characteristics and other factors (P<0.05).</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">A total of 275 students responded (men: 55.6%, women: 44.4%), with 50.9% studying at the Foundation of Science and 49.1% at the Foundation of Science and Technology (FIST). The majority had mild-to-severe depression (56.4%) and anxiety (65.5%); 26.2% were stressed, and 10.2% engaged in NES. NES was not significantly associated with sex, age, monthly pocket money or body mass index. A significant number of students with NES were from the FIST (P=0.036). The factors significantly related to NES were depression (P=0.003), anxiety (P=0.021), stress (P<0.001), poor sleep quality (P=0.001) and risk of eating disorders (P=0.003).</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">NES should be screened among at-risk college students to ensure they receive appropriate treatment.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© Academy of Family Physicians of Malaysia.</CopyrightInformation></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author This study investigated the potential effects of Imperatorin (IMP), a furocoumarin and a phytochemical isolated from the leaves of <i>Ferulago trifida</i> on valproic acid (VPA)-induced behavioral and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) alterations in a rat model of ASD. Open field test (locomotion, anxiety), grooming test, marble burying test (OCD-like behavior), novel object recognition memory test, and real-time PCR (BDNF levels) were conducted to collect data. The results showed increased locomotion in ASD-like rats in both sexes with greater effect in females, while IMP restored it in males and decreased it in females. Anxiety was increased in ASD-like rats in both sexes with greater effect in females; IMP had no effect. Grooming was increased in ASD-like rats in both sexes with greater effect in females, while IMP restored it in males and decreased it in females. Marbles buried was increased in ASD-like rats in both sexes, while IMP decreased it in males. Memory was impaired in ASD-like rats in both sexes; IMP had no effect. BDNF was decreased in ASD-like rats in both sexes with greater effect in females, while IMP increased it in both sexes. In conclusion, our findings showed hyperlocomotion, anxiety-like behavior, OCD-like behavior, memory deficit, and BDNF downregulation as ASD-related features, with evidence of sex-specific patterns and partial therapeutic effects of IMP.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© 2026 The Authors.</CopyrightInformation></Abstract><AuthorList CompleteYN="Y"><Author ValidYN="Y"><LastName>Mohamadian</LastName><ForeName>Marjan</ForeName><Initials>M</Initials><AffiliationInfo><Affiliation>School of Behavioral Sciences, California Southern University, Costa Mesa, CA, USA.</Affiliation></AffiliationInfo></Author><Author ValidYN="Y"><LastName>Barzi</LastName><ForeName>Fatemeh</ForeName><Initials>F</Initials><AffiliationInfo><Affiliation>Department of Cognitive Psychology, Institute for Cognitive and Brain Sciences, Shahid Beheshti University, Tehran, Iran.</Affiliation></AffiliationInfo></Author><Author ValidYN="Y"><LastName>Jalalian-Javadpour</LastName><ForeName>Marzieh</ForeName><Initials>M</Initials><AffiliationInfo><Affiliation>Department of Cell and Molecular Biology, Faculty of Medical Sciences, TeMS.C. Traditional instruction heavily leans on abstract symbols, which can add to cognitive load and a feeling of emotional opposition. To address this issue, this study developed a learning model integrating augmented reality (AR) and haptic feedback to create an interactive and multisensory mathematics experience. A quasi-experimental design was conducted with 120 students divided into experimental and control groups. The experimental group used the AR-haptic mathematics game for six weeks, while the control group learned through textbooks and teacher explanations. Data was gathered by using the conceptual understanding tests, a mathematics anxiety scale, classroom observations and student interviews. The quantitative data were analyzed by t-test, ANCOVA and MANOVA analysis; qualitative data were analyzed positionally. The results indicated significant progress in experimental groups' conceptual understanding and mathematics anxiety decrease when compared to the control group. The mean for the post-test experimental group was 82, and for the control group, it was 62 with a large effect size. The average level of maths anxiety decreased in the experimental group from 3.2 to 1.8 on a five-point scale. Qualitative feedback revealed that students found the game engaging, enjoyable, and less intimidating than traditional lessons. The integration of AR and haptic feedback effectively enhanced both cognitive and affective outcomes in mathematics learning. The multisensory environment enabled students to interact with abstract concepts in tangible ways, reducing anxiety and promoting positive attitudes toward mathematics. This provides a proof of concept for the effectiveness of immersive technologies as assistive tools in the enhancement of academic achievement and emotional health related to elementary level ValidYN="Y">1666</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.1186/s12909-026-10050-y</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">Anatomy education increasingly incorporates digital and simulation-based resources alongside cadaver-based instruction; however, uncertainty remains regarding how different modalities can be integrated to support both cognitive learning and emotional adaptation. This study compared the effects of prosection, plastic model-based practice, and Acland's Video Atlas of Human Anatomy on medical students' learning outcomes and experiences.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHOD" NlmCategory="METHODS">A prospective crossover within-subjects design was conducted with 45 first-year medical students who sequentially experienced three instructional modalities across two anatomy topics. Following theoretical lectures, students participated in practical sessions using prosection, plastic models, and Acland's Video Atlas. Pre- and post-tests assessed theoretical and practical knowledge. A feedback questionnaire including Likert-scale and open-ended questions evaluated students' emotional responses, learning experiences, and instructional preferences. Qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">All groups demonstrated significant improvement between pre- and post-test scores (p < 0.05), with no significant between-group differences in theoretical, practical, or total post-test scores. Tool-specific performance gains were observed in cadaver- and video-based assessment items. Qualitative analysis identified three main themes: self-development, learning strategies and method preferences, and evaluation of instructional modalities. Students described a gradual transition from anxiety and uncertainty toward familiarity, confidence, and engagement. They also emphasized the complementary roles of videos, plastic models, and cadaver-based learning.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">Comparable cognitive outcomes across modalities suggest that learning effectiveness depends more on pedagogical integration than on the instructional medium itself. Multimodal anatomy learning appears to support knowledge acquisition while fostering positive learning experiences, and authentic engagement with anatomy.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© 2026. Vitamin A promotes immunity, neurogenesis, energy balance, and gut integrity. However, most studies have focused on early developmental stages and adult-onset VAD remain poorly understood.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="OBJECTIVE" NlmCategory="OBJECTIVE">To determine whether physiological, behavioural, and gut microbial responses to adult-onset VAD differ between male and female rats.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">Adult male and female Wistar rats (9-10 weeks) were fed a vitamin A-sufficient (VAS, n = 6) or VAD (n = 6) diet for 20 weeks. Vitamin A levels were monitored every 4 weeks. Behavioural function was assessed at 12th and 18th weeks. After 20 weeks, rats were euthanised, and serum, cecal contents, liver, duodenum, hippocampus, and visceral white adipose tissue (vWAT) were collected for assessment of vitamin A metabolites, physiological and morphological changes, gut microbiome, and serum metabolome. Data were analysed using Student's t-test or the Mann-Whitney U test, as appropriate, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">Females and males reach the deficiency threshold (<0.7 μmol/L) at 12 and 16 weeks, respectively. At week 12, females showed a 2-fold reduction in serum vitamin A levels (VAS, 1.1 vs VAD, 0.5 μmol/L;p = 0.012), despite unchanged body weight and feed intake. Microbial responses were sex-divergent; the Bacillota/Bacteroidota ratio increased only in females (4.18 in VAS vs 7.0 in VAD; p = 0.008). The virome shifted in both sexes, with distinct signatures. Anxiety-like behaviour appears by 12 weeks in females but not in males. Systemic responses (reduced gut barrier, increased immune gene expression, and adipocyte hypertrophy) were largely shared.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSIONS" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">This study provides evidence that adult-onset VAD in rats may be associated with sex-specific alterations in the microbiome, but with more generalised systemic outcomes.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026.
